_meta.notes: Hawaiian names verified against Nā Inoa Hōkū (Johnson & Mahelona, Bishop Museum). See corrections_log for name changes from v2.0. Confirm with a cultural advisor before public deployment.

categories.nav: Primary Navigation Star — used for bearing and latitude
categories.seasonal: Seasonal Marker — marks calendar events or seasons
categories.starline: Star Line — one of the Nā Lālani Hōkū navigation arcs
categories.planet: Planet — hōkū ʻeleʻele, the moving stars

stars.meaning: "Star of Gladness" — zenith star of Hawaiʻi at 21°N
stars.navRole: Tahitian navigators sailed north following Hōkūleʻa to reach Hawaiʻi. It passes directly overhead at 21°N — the latitude of the islands. The voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa is named for it. When Hōkūleʻa is at zenith, you are at the latitude of Hawaiʻi.
stars.obsNote: Tracked by UH 2.2m & Keck; spectral data in IRTF Maunakea archives.

stars.meaning: "Fixed Star" — the unmoving anchor of the northern sky
stars.riseHouse: Circumpolar — never sets at Hawaiʻi latitude
stars.navRole: The North Star. Its altitude above the horizon equals your latitude north of the equator — at Hawaiʻi it sits about 20° up. Kept astern when sailing south to Tahiti. When it disappears below the horizon, you have crossed the equator — switch to the Southern Cross.
stars.obsNote: Used as a calibration reference star for Maunakea telescope pointing systems.

stars.meaning: "Glowing / Burning" — the brightest star in the Hawaiian sky
stars.navRole: Brightest star in the Hawaiian sky. Passes directly over the latitude of Tahiti (17°S) — used to navigate the return voyage south. Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi star line. Its heliacal rising signals the beginning of the fishing season.
stars.obsNote: One of the nearest stars to Earth. Extensively studied at Keck for stellar atmosphere properties.

stars.meaning: "Eyes of the Chief" — marks the start of Makahiki, the Hawaiian New Year
stars.navRole: Rising of Makaliʻi at sunset marks the start of Makahiki — the Hawaiian New Year and four-month festival season. Critical seasonal marker. Gives its name to the star line Ke Kā o Makaliʻi. Also used as a latitude check — its altitude shifts predictably as you sail north or south.
stars.obsNote: Extensively imaged by Subaru Telescope on Maunakea. Part of UKIRT infrared surveys.

stars.meaning: "The Great Fishhook of Māui" — with which Māui fished up the Hawaiian Islands
stars.navRole: The entire constellation serves as a southern meridian pointer. When the fishhook is at its highest in the south, the navigator knows true south. The heart — Antares, called Lehua — confirms the bearing. Dominant sky feature of the Kau (dry) season.
stars.obsNote: Antares monitored by Keck for stellar mass loss. UKIRT infrared tracks dust shells around this supergiant.

stars.meaning: "Blossom" — flowering before the great Dog Star rises
stars.navRole: Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc. Rises before Sirius and helps track the curvature of this key star group across the sky. Its position relative to Sirius gives the navigator a sense of the arc's orientation.
stars.obsNote: High-resolution spectroscopy conducted at Keck I, Maunakea.

stars.meaning: "Cared for by the Moon" — a child of the Moon
stars.navRole: The Southern Cross takes over from Hōkūpaʻa once the navigator crosses the equator. Two pointer stars — Alpha and Beta Centauri — indicate its position. The long axis of the cross points to the south celestial pole. Ka Iwikuamoʻo (the Backbone star line) runs from Polaris through Arcturus all the way down to the Southern Cross.
stars.obsNote: Low elevation from Maunakea. CFHT archive includes Crux region southern sky surveys.

stars.meaning: "Star Wreath" — northernmost star of the Makaliʻi arc
stars.navRole: Northernmost star of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc. Helps the navigator track the full curvature of this key star line from north to south across the winter sky.
stars.obsNote: Binary star resolved with Keck interferometry at Maunakea.

stars.meaning: "The Kite" — anchor of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line
stars.navRole: Anchor of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line — the Kite of Kāwelo. Rises nearly due northeast and sets nearly due northwest, making it an excellent compass reference. One of the brightest stars in the summer sky.
stars.obsNote: Vega was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed. Studied at Keck for debris disk structure.

stars.meaning: "The Standing One" — swift-rising equatorial star
stars.navRole: Rises almost exactly due east and sets almost exactly due west — making it one of the most reliable compass stars for east-west bearings. Part of the summer triangle alongside Vega and Deneb. Rotates so rapidly it is visibly flattened at its poles.
stars.obsNote: Altair is close enough that its surface has been directly imaged — one of very few stars where this is possible.

stars.meaning: "The Tail" — tail of the great celestial bird
stars.navRole: Third point of the summer triangle. Despite being thousands of light years away, Deneb shines brightly because it is one of the most luminous stars known. Useful northern compass reference in the summer and fall sky.
stars.obsNote: Deneb is so distant its exact distance is uncertain — between 1,500 and 2,600 light years. Studied at Keck for its powerful stellar wind.

stars.meaning: "Look Behind" (Nana-hope) — second of the Na Mahoe twin stars
stars.navRole: Second of the Na Mahoe (Twin) stars in the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc — Pollux (β Geminorum). Rises after Nānāmua (Castor). Together they bracket a section of the winter star line.
stars.obsNote: Pollux is the nearest giant star to our solar system. It hosts a confirmed exoplanet — Pollux b.

stars.meaning: "Look Forward" (Nana-mua) — first of the Na Mahoe twin stars
stars.spec: A1 V + A2 Vm Sextuple System
stars.navRole: First of the Na Mahoe (Twin) stars in the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc — Castor (α Geminorum). Rises just north of its twin Nānahope (Pollux). Johnson & Mahelona record this pair as Nānāmua and Nānahope.
stars.obsNote: Castor's six-star system has been resolved by interferometry. Studied at the CFHT on Maunakea.

stars.meaning: "The Fishhook from the Heavens" — the divine hook of Māui
stars.spec: B1 III-IV + B2 V Binary (Blue Giants)
stars.navRole: Zenith star for the Marquesas Islands — when Spica is directly overhead, you are at the latitude of the Marquesas, the likely origin point of the Hawaiian migration. Anchor of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line in the spring sky.
stars.obsNote: A close binary system — the two blue giants orbit each other every four days, distorting each other into egg shapes.

stars.meaning: "The Black Fish Trap" — a dark southern constellation
stars.navRole: A compact, distinctive southern constellation used as a pointer toward Spica. Part of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line region. Its dark, trapezoid shape is recognizable even in moderately bright skies and helps the navigator locate the spring star line.
stars.obsNote: Corvus region studied for background galaxy surveys using CFHT wide-field imaging.

stars.meaning: "The Mouth of the Southern Fish" — lone bright star of the southern autumn sky
stars.navRole: One of the few bright stars in the southern autumn sky, making it a critical latitude reference when sailing south. Its low position on the southern horizon from Hawaiʻi means its visibility is directly tied to sky darkness — a dark sky benchmark star.
stars.obsNote: Fomalhaut hosts one of the most photographed debris disks in astronomy — imaged by Hubble and studied at Maunakea for exoplanet candidates.

stars.meaning: "Fine Braided Cord" — second brightest star in the sky
stars.navRole: Second brightest star in the entire sky after Sirius. Barely visible from Hawaiʻi — it skims the southern horizon. Its altitude above the horizon tells a navigator precisely how far south of Hawaiʻi they have sailed. When Canopus is high in the sky, you are in the southern latitudes near Tahiti.
stars.obsNote: Canopus is used as a navigation reference star by spacecraft — including the Voyager probes. Its extreme brightness despite great distance means it is a true supergiant.

stars.meaning: "The Pointer" — guides the eye to the Southern Cross
stars.spec: G2 V + K1 V Binary (Sun-like stars)
stars.navRole: The nearest star system to our Sun. Together with Beta Centauri, it forms the two Pointer Stars that indicate the Southern Cross. When the navigator is south of the equator and needs to find south, they locate the Pointers and follow them to Hānaiakamālama.
stars.obsNote: The nearest star system to Earth at 4.37 light years. Proxima Centauri — its third companion — is even closer at 4.24 light years and hosts a candidate exoplanet.

stars.meaning: "The Seven" — seven stars that point to Hōkūpaʻa
stars.navRole: The two outer stars of the Dipper bowl — Dubhe and Merak — are called the Pointer Stars and point directly to Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris). Multiply the distance between them by five to find the North Star. Nā Hiku is circumpolar from Hawaiʻi, meaning it never sets and can be used any clear night of the year.
stars.obsNote: Several Big Dipper stars are part of the Ursa Major Moving Group — a cluster of stars born together that have since drifted apart. Studied at UH 2.2m telescope.

stars.meaning: "The Sacred Lehua Blossom" — red heart of the Fishhook
stars.navRole: The red heart of Ka Makau Nui o Māui. Its deep red color — visible to the naked eye — made it culturally significant across Polynesia. At its highest point in the south it confirms true south bearing. Mars occasionally passes close to Antares — ancient Polynesian navigators would have noted this rare conjunction.
stars.obsNote: If placed at the center of our solar system, Antares would extend beyond the orbit of Mars. Monitored at Keck for stellar mass loss through its powerful stellar wind.

stars.w: Star Line: Capella → Pollux → Procyon → Sirius
stars.meaning: "The Canoe-Bailer of Makaliʻi" — the great winter navigation arc
stars.navRole: The primary winter star line. The arc runs from Capella (Hōkūleī) in the north through the Pleiades (Makaliʻi), Pollux (Nānahope), Procyon (Puana), and down to Sirius (Aʻā). This line sweeps across the sky like a giant canoe bailer — the navigator tracks the whole arc to confirm bearing and latitude simultaneously. Dominant from November through March.
stars.obsNote: This star line was central to Nainoa Thompson's revival of Hawaiian navigation in the 1970s-80s, developed in consultation at the Bishop Museum Planetarium.

stars.w: Star Line: Polaris → Arcturus → Southern Cross
stars.meaning: "The Backbone" — the great north-south spine of the sky
stars.navRole: The great north-south axis of Hawaiian navigation. Runs from Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris) in the north through Nā Hiku (Big Dipper), down through Hōkūleʻa (Arcturus) at zenith, and all the way south to Hānaiakamālama (the Southern Cross). A navigator who can see this full line knows their exact orientation — it is a complete compass in itself.
stars.obsNote: This star line spans the entire sky from north to south — a remarkable feat of observation that required many voyages to map completely.

stars.w: Star Line: Vega → Altair → Spica → Corvus
stars.meaning: "The Kite of Kāwelo" — the great spring and summer star line
stars.navRole: The spring and summer star line shaped like a kite. Runs from Vega (Kāwelo) in the north through Altair (Kēkūaʻōnohi) and down to Spica (Mānaiakalani) and Corvus (Hinaʻeleʻele) in the south. Used when Ke Kā o Makaliʻi has set below the horizon — the seasonal transition between these two lines tells the navigator which half of the year they are in.
stars.obsNote: Ka Lupe o Kāwelo is one of the four Nā Lālani Hōkū — the four Hawaiian star lines that together provide 24-hour sky coverage for navigation.

stars.w: Star Line: Scorpius arc through southern sky
stars.meaning: "The Fishhook from Heaven" — the great southern star line
stars.navRole: The great southern star line following the arc of Scorpius across the sky. Dominant in the summer sky when Ke Kā o Makaliʻi is absent. The curving shape mirrors the fishhook shape of Māui's hook — the navigator reads the whole arc, not just individual stars, to maintain bearing across the southern ocean.
stars.obsNote: The four Nā Lālani Hōkū — Ke Kā o Makaliʻi, Ka Iwikuamoʻo, Ka Lupe o Kāwelo, and Manaiakalani — together provide continuous navigational reference through every season and every hour of the night.

stars.meaning: "The Star That Steers the Canoe" — the dawn and dusk navigator
stars.spec: Planet — brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon
stars.riseHouse: Varies — rises and sets within 3 hours of the Sun
stars.navRole: The most important planet for Polynesian navigation. Appears as the brilliant Evening Star in the west after sunset, or as the Morning Star in the east before dawn — providing a precise bearing at the two most critical navigation moments of the day. Never strays far from the Sun's path, making its rising and setting direction a reliable east-west compass reference.
stars.obsNote: Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon. Its phases can be seen with the naked eye. Pioneer Venus and Magellan spacecraft data archived and studied at IfA Hawaiʻi.

stars.meaning: "The Chief" — brightest of the wandering stars
stars.navRole: The brightest true star-like object in the night sky (after Venus). Moves slowly enough against the background stars that it can be used as a temporary compass reference for weeks at a time. Hawaiian navigators would have used Jupiter as a moving but predictable beacon — its position relative to fixed stars confirmed latitude and season.
stars.obsNote: Jupiter and its moons are extensively studied at Keck Observatory. The Great Red Spot storm is monitored for long-term changes.

stars.meaning: "The Red Star" — the wandering fire star
stars.spec: Planet — red from iron oxide surface
stars.navRole: Its unmistakable red-orange color — similar to Antares (Lehua) — made Mars culturally significant. Ancient navigators were careful not to confuse Mars with Antares, especially when Mars passed near the Scorpius region. This near-conjunction was a notable celestial event. Mars moves faster than Jupiter, requiring more frequent position updates.
stars.obsNote: Mars surface features are studied using Maunakea telescopes during opposition. The IRTF on Maunakea specializes in Mars atmospheric observations.

stars.meaning: "The Slow One" — the patient wanderer
stars.navRole: The slowest-moving of the visible planets — it takes approximately 29 years to complete one circuit of the sky. This slow, steady movement made it a reliable long-term seasonal marker. A navigator who knew where Saturn was at the start of a voyage could use its position to track the passage of time over a multi-week journey.
stars.obsNote: Saturn's rings and moons are studied extensively at Keck. The Cassini spacecraft mission was planned in part using Maunakea observations.

stars.w: Milky Way (Te Ara o Tama-nui-te-rā / Māpunapuna)
stars.meaning: "The Long Coral Reef in the Sky" — the great river of stars
stars.navRole: The Milky Way arch itself served as a navigation reference — its orientation across the sky changes predictably through the night and through the seasons. When the galactic center rises in the southeast, the navigator knows the summer sky orientation. Polynesian cultures across the Pacific had names for the Milky Way and incorporated it into navigation and seasonal calendars.
stars.obsNote: The dark skies of Maunakea are essential for studying the Milky Way's structure. Subaru Telescope's wide-field surveys are mapping billions of Milky Way stars.

stars.meaning: "The Best" — top star of Hānaiakamālama (Southern Cross)
stars.navRole: Top star of the Southern Cross (Hānaiakamālama). With Ka Mole Honua (Acrux) it points toward the south celestial pole. Named in Nā Inoa Hōkū as part of the cross asterism used south of the equator.
stars.obsNote: Part of the Crux asterism — low elevation from Maunakea; southern sky surveys at CFHT.

stars.meaning: "The Barren Lands" — brightest star of the Southern Cross
stars.navRole: Brightest star of Hānaiakamālama — the bottom of the cross points to the south celestial pole. Primary southern bearing star when sailing below the equator. Also referenced as the heart of navigation below Hawaiʻi latitude.
stars.obsNote: Same region as Hānaiakamālama/Crux — extensively catalogued in southern hemisphere surveys.

stars.meaning: "Dawn" — swiftest of the wandering stars
stars.navRole: Mercury never strays far from the Sun — visible only near dawn or dusk. Hawaiian navigators would have noted its rapid motion against the background stars as a distinctive hōkū ʻeleʻele (wandering star).
stars.obsNote: Studied by planetary astronomers; IfA Hawaiʻi hosts planetary science programs.

stars.meaning: "Moon" — ruler of the Kaulana Mahina lunar calendar
stars.navRole: The Moon governs the Kaulana Mahina — 30 named nights per month. Moon phase and brightness directly affect which navigation stars are visible; bright moonlight can reduce naked-eye limiting magnitude by 1–2.5 magnitudes.
stars.obsNote: Lunar phases calculated in this app's Kaulana Mahina tab; critical for planning sky brightness readings.
